rv.q: It’s been years—decades, really—since I last saw production numbers that were infused with the kind of rich, sustained creativity that Mr. Wheeldon gives us throughout “An American in Paris.”
This gorgeously danced — and just plain gorgeous — production pays loving tribute to the 1951 movie.
The exuberant new musical is helmed with panache by top director and choreographer Christopher Wheeldon.
Just how extraordinary is unspooled all evening with exuberant, sweeping innovation, dark historical understanding and a big, smart heart.
The same might be said of this unorthodox transformation of a bright and cheerful All
The conjoining of these worlds on Broadway makes for one very fortunate collision.
Barring a trip across the Atlantic, there’s probably no better way to visit Paris this spring.
As directed by the choreographer Christopher Wheeldon and starring the dancers Robert Fairchild and Leanne Cope, An American in Paris is a fine and fanciful entertainment.
An American in Paris is a show that dances its way into your heart with gorgeous choreography and sumptuous design.
When those two are onstage, they make you believe in love — and the power of dance — all over again.
There are no surprises, of either the negative or the especially positive sort.
And while one is always grateful to hear them and to see artists at work with serious ideas, the result seems self-cancelling.
There's much gorgeous ballet to admire but the overall effect is of a dance concert with a semiserious musical squeezed into the cracks.
But only then does it fully work.
In Paris is a thrilling addition to Broadway.
Like this American In Paris overall, it's a dazzling achievement in its own right.
And the dancing in this new An American in Paris is sublime.
Regardless of the book, the music is glorious, the visuals are innovative and the performances are top-rate.
An American in Paris is as smart and spirited as it is spectacular.
Dance is the only language really needed here.
Might we credit Christopher Wheeldon with presenting dance as one way to bring new light to the Broadway stage?

A dancer is a thing of beauty, and there is beaucoup beauty in director-choreographer Christopher Wheeldon's ravishing production of 'An American in Paris,' smartly but not slavishly adapted by Craig Lucas from the 1951 MGM movie.
Whether the cast is pirouetting and on toe or doing synchronized high kicks a la Busby Berkeley, the movements are elegant and energetic, witty and romantic.
As I say, you see this An American in Paris for the dancing.
An excellent showcase for the talents of ballet fixture Christopher Wheeldon, who makes his Broadway debut as director and choreographer.
And yet…would that there were more!
But when the dancing stops, it falls disappointingly flat.
Someone forgot to put the American in this “Paris.”
An American in Paris, one of the best musicals in recent memory.
This is not your typical Broadway musical — this is ballet set upon a Broadway stage, and it is simply remarkable.

This marvelous cast and ensemble cast all take a leading role in this exquisite production that will leave you standing on your feet, violently clapping, smiling from ear to ear with tears rolling down your cheeks.
The generally dreamy quality with which Wheeldon imbues the production results in a thoroughly enchanting attraction.
The production achieves an integration of artistic and creative elements that is thoroughly realised.
And so it is with An American in Paris; the fusion of the Broadway musical and ballet, set to the sublime music and lyrics of the Gershwin Brothers’ songbook, is an evening of pure enchantment.
And over half a century later, the wait was worth every minute.
The final product feels to be a patchwork musical, indulging the audience with visual spectacles and beloved melodies at the expense of cohesive musical storytelling.

What this creative team has brought to a Broadway season currently awash in musical revivals is something innovative yet familiar, a gorgeous and moving tribute that emerges as a triumph for a new day.

While it’s impossible to dislike An American in Paris, it must be said that the show coasts on the familiarity of the songs and the stunning choreography which sometimes makes one wonder if it would’ve worked best as a full on ballet rather than a Broadway musical.
I did my best to focus on what was happening on-stage, but it was hard to find any of it compelling.

cn.t: Critics praise Christopher Wheeldon's breathtaking choreography and gorgeous visuals, though some find the romance lacking emotional depth. The ballet-driven production showcases spectacular dancing but divides opinion on its storytelling.

sg.ra: After the 2023 TSX lift the orchestra received wider seats and a slight rake, and center rows G-K are the unobstructed sweet spot before the mezzanine overhang begins at Row K per the official chart; AVFMS reports suggest the overhang only becomes visually noticeable closer to Row N-O, so center G-K is the cleanest post-reno picture.

sg.vl: Discount seats but mezz starts to bite
sg.ra: The mezzanine overhang begins cutting in roughly at Orchestra Row K per the theatre's official seating chart, so rear-orchestra tickets (Row N onward) are priced well below center-premium but you give up the top of the proscenium; one AVFMS reviewer at Row N seat 119 still reported no overhang intrusion, so the rear orch is a real value play on non-spectacle shows that don't use high flying scenery.

Post-2023 lift reviewers specifically call out that the front-mezz sightline is 'incredible' and gives a panoramic view of the choreography, and multiple sources name center Rows A-C (or middle C-F) as the unobstructed sweet spot; avoid the first two side-aisle seats in Row A which Broadway Direct flags as obstructed by a safety railing that survived the renovation.

Unlike most Broadway houses, the Palace rear mezz sits on the same elevated tier rather than under a balcony overhang, so sightlines stay open to the top of the proscenium even at the back — a November 2025 AVFMS reviewer confirmed you are 'pretty high up but atleast you have a full view of the stage'; the tradeoff is distance plus the tight 1920s row spacing the reno preserved.

The Palace's mezz-level boxes are routinely sold as obstructed-view and nytix explicitly warns 'the box seats are not recommended, as they do not provide a clear view of the stage' — the severe side angle means upstage-left blocking is cut off; pick them only if you want the close-in vibe over actually seeing the full stage picture, and never for a dance-heavy or spectacle title.

The balcony survived the lift essentially unchanged — nytix flags that 'the view from the first row of the balcony may be blocked by a large horizontal bar, so sitting in the rows behind the first row is recommended,' and post-reno reviewers still call the balcony 'pretty far' from stage; there is no step-free access, so even the cheapest seat carries real friction.
